html:
The killing of Julius Caesar, dictator of Rome, by a group of senators on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE. They stabbed him 23 times at a meeting of the Senate in the hall of the Theatre of Pompey.

Caesar had won a civil war against Pompey and the Senate, and early in 44 BCE he was named dictator for life. To many senators this looked like a return of kings, hated in Rome since 509 BCE. Some sixty men joined the plot, led by Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius, some of whom Caesar had pardoned.

The plotters hoped to restore the Republic but had no plan for what came next. Crowds turned against them at Caesar's funeral, where Mark Antony spoke. Caesar's heir, his great-nephew Octavian, joined Antony; they outlawed their enemies, among them Cicero, and beat Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BCE. Octavian then defeated Antony and became Augustus, the first emperor. A murder meant to save the Republic ended it.
sum: The killing of Julius Caesar, dictator of Rome, by a group of senators on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE. They stabbed him 23 times at a meeting of the Senate in the hall of the Theatre of Pompey.
